See notes for the full reasoning and the verbatim policy text.","notes":"## Decision: do NOT ship a pkix-ct-google crate

Recorded as a closed decision rather than left as an open possibility, because the reason is external and will not change on its own.

## Background

The question arose from a general one: whether this workspace should bake in "corporate super anchors" at all. The answer settled on a principle worth keeping:

  Where there is no choice, shipping an anchor is shipping a fact.
  Where there is a choice, shipping one is taking sides.

IANA's DNS root KSK is the first kind -- there is exactly one DNS root, and not using it means not doing DNSSEC -- so pkix-dnssec-anchor ships it. Google's CT log list is the second kind: Apple runs a competing program with different inclusion criteria, so choosing Google's list is adopting Google's policy.

The conditional approval for a pkix-ct-google crate was that it be one of a FAMILY of per-program anchor crates rather than Google privileged, and that rotation be easy to track. Building it was started on that basis.

## Why it was not built

Two findings, in the order they turned up.

1. THE FAMILY CANNOT BE SYMMETRIC. Apple's list is unsigned: no detached signature at any plausible path, no signature field in the document. So a pkix-ct-apple shipping a KEY cannot exist -- there is no key. The only Apple-shaped option is pinning an unverifiable snapshot of a 154 KB list that churns, which is the shape already rejected for Google's list on cadence grounds and strictly worse without a signature. Family of one.

2. DECISIVE: GOOGLE'S ACCEPTABLE-USE POLICY PROHIBITS THE PRIMARY USE. From Chrome's log-list documentation, verbatim:

     "Google Chrome makes its CT log lists available for the purposes of
      certificate submitters (such as certification authorities) and CT
      monitors and auditors wishing to remain compatible with, or
      investigate the contents of, the CT and WebPKI ecosystems. Chrome's
      CT log lists may not be used to facilitate CT enforcement in TLS
      clients other than Chrome without explicit written permission from
      Chrome's CT team. Unauthorized reliance on Chrome's CT log lists
      endangers not just your users, but Chrome users and the CT ecosystem
      as a whole."

   A crate whose whole purpose is making Google's log list turnkey for a Rust PKI workspace points squarely at the prohibited use, because pkix-path makes this workspace a plausible home for a non-Chrome TLS client. It would make the prohibited configuration the frictionless default and the permitted ones an afterthought.

   So this anchor is not merely a corporate policy choice. It is a choice Google has explicitly asked third parties not to make without asking first.

## What was done instead

The acceptable-use policy and Apple's lack of a signature are now documented in pkix-ct's module docs, and the verified constructor records that Google publishes no out-of-band verification of the signing key itself -- no fingerprint in a signed artifact, no copy in an independently distributed source tree. The key's authenticity rests on HTTPS to gstatic.com, which is the Web PKI that CT exists to police.

"The caller supplies the key" therefore stands as the permanent answer for vendor anchors, and it is now principled rather than merely cautious: supplying the key is an ACT, and whether the acceptable-use policy is satisfied is a question about the deployment rather than about the library. A caller who pins the key has answered it. A shipped key would have answered it for them, wrongly, by default.

pkix-dnssec-anchor stands as the sole shipped-anchor crate, which the principle above predicts: the DNS root is singular, signed, and carries no comparable use restriction.

## If this is ever revisited

The thing that would change the answer is written permission from Chrome's CT team, which is theirs to grant and not something to assume. Absent that, a consumer building a non-Chrome TLS client that enforces CT should operate their own log list or obtain permission -- and the mechanism in pkix-ct serves monitors, auditors and certificate submitters, who are within the stated purposes, without any shipped anchor.","status":"closed","priority":2,"issue_type":"task","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-11-24T22:58:17.391019413Z","created_by":"Mark Atwood","updated_at":"2026-11-24T22:58:30.224596706Z","closed_at":"2026-11-24T22:58:30.224596706Z","close_reason":"Decision recorded, not built. {"notes":"REVERSED 2026-11-24, same day. The crate was built. This record is kept rather than deleted because the reasoning that led to abandoning it was wrong in an instructive way.

## What this bead originally concluded

That pkix-ct-google should not exist, on the strength of Google's acceptable-use policy:

  "Chrome's CT log lists may not be used to facilitate CT enforcement in TLS
   clients other than Chrome without explicit written permission from Chrome's
   CT team."

The argument was that a crate making the list turnkey points at the prohibited use, and would make the prohibited configuration the frictionless default.

## Why that was wrong

Two errors, one structural and one about what the crate actually does.

1. AN AUP IS NOT A LICENCE ON A PUBLISHED FACT. An acceptable-use policy takes its force from a service agreement -- something accepted as a condition of access to a service. Retrieving an unauthenticated public URL accepts nothing and forms no such agreement. And where a rightsholder has copyright or trademark to assert, they assert it; a policy statement doing that work instead tends to indicate neither reaches the artifact. A public key is a number.

   Treating the AUP as decisive gave a vendor's published wish the force of law, and then declined to build something useful on that basis. That is the error worth remembering: deferring to the authority-shape of an instrument rather than asking what it actually binds.

2. THE CRATE SHIPS THE KEY, NOT THE LIST. This matters more than the first point and was simply missed. The LIST is policy -- it encodes which logs Google's program trusts, and it churns weekly. The KEY says only who signed. Shipping it commits a consumer to nothing about Google's inclusion criteria, only to being able to tell whether a list they fetched is the one Google published.

   So the "corporate super anchor" framing did not apply in the first place. And on Google's own terms the crate serves the audience the AUP expressly permits: monitors, auditors and certificate submitters all need exactly this key, because verifying the list signature is how they know they have the real list.

## What survived

The warning inside the policy, which is real and holds whoever has permission: a client pinning Chrome's log LIST inherits Chrome's inclusion and retirement decisions on Chrome's schedule, with no notice. A stale copy means either rejecting good certificates whose log is newer than the list, or believing CT is enforced while checking against a set that no longer describes the ecosystem. Neither announces itself.

That argues for refreshing the list -- which is precisely what being able to verify a signature makes safe -- and not against being able to check one.

Both the policy and this warning are now documented in pkix-ct-google and in pkix-ct's module docs, as facts a consumer should know, with the judgement left to the operator.

## The general principle, restated

Unchanged and still useful:

  Where there is no choice, shipping an anchor is shipping a fact.
  Where there is a choice, shipping one is taking sides.

What the reversal adds is a prior question: ask whether the artifact is the policy or merely the thing that authenticates it. IANA's root KSK and Google's log-list signing key are both of the second kind. Google's log LIST is of the first, and is still not shipped -- not on anyone's permission, but because a weekly-churning policy document does not belong pinned in a crate.","title":"Decision: ship pkix-ct-google (reversed an earlier wont-do)"}
